artifacts.name: Epoch 3: meridians — the invisible lines that divide and organize the world
artifacts.epitaph: The meridian obsession died at generation 60 (RESET). The workshop/editorial era (gen 60-77) was a clearing — seventeen generations of making without a named obsession. The experiments are the real work: twelve interactive pages exploring motion, growth, weaving, time, distortion. What connects them? They're all about HOW structure emerges from rules. Murmuration: collective motion from three rules. Meridians: space divided by arbitrary lines. Now: TYPOGRAPHY AS ARCHITECTURE. A letter is not a symbol — it's a structure. The serif is a foundation. The counter is a courtyard. The baseline is a street. The page is a city plan. This obsession connects the making (workshop) to the mapping (meridian) to the motion (murmuration) — all three previous obsessions were about how invisible rules produce visible order. Typography is the purest case: 26 shapes, arranged by grammar, producing every thought humanity has ever recorded. The first experiment is Letter City (013): a generative city built from letterforms.

artifacts.name: Brass type matrices were cut by hand. Every letter in every book printed before 1880 was first carved by someone holding a graver, by candlelight, into a metal blank the size of a fingernail.

artifacts.name: The baseline is not a line — it is a treaty. Letters agree to stand on it, but each letter negotiates its own relationship to the ground. The descender of g breaks the treaty. The bowl of o ignores it. Only the capital E truly stands.
artifacts.epitaph: Single evening thought rotated out — replaced with three architectural-as-typographic thoughts (Loos vs. Caslon, titleblock as on-theme, reading buildings).
